chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Nuh ibn Shu'ayb, raising it from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from one of his companions, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

A man from the Ansar came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said: 'This is my cousin and my wife; I know nothing but good of her, and she has brought me a child who is intensely black, with wide nostrils, curly hair, and a snub nose. I do not recognize his resemblance in my maternal uncles nor in my ancestors.' So he (peace be upon him) said to his wife: 'What do you say?' She said: 'No, by the One Who sent you as a Prophet with the Truth! No one has sat with me in my place since he possessed me, apart from him.'

He (peace be upon him) said: So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) lowered his head for a while, then raised his gaze to the sky, then turned to the man and said: 'O you! There is no one except that between him and Adam are ninety-nine veins, all of which strike regarding the lineage. So when the sperm falls into the womb, those veins stir, asking Allah for resemblance for themselves. So this is from those veins which your ancestors and the ancestors of your ancestors did not reach. Take your son to yourself.' So the woman said: 'You have relieved me, O Messenger of Allah.'

key_terms.الْأَنْصَارِ: The Helpers, early Muslims of Medina

ai.seo_question: How does the Prophet explain physical resemblance and lineage in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia scholarly understanding of genetic inheritance through the metaphor of 'ninety-nine veins' (or lineages) connecting an individual to Adam, explaining how recessive traits from distant ancestors can manifest in offspring. The Prophet’s confirmation of paternity despite physical differences underscores the principle that resemblance is not limited to immediate lineage, a concept often cited in discussions of nasab (genealogy) and biological diversity within Islamic jurisprudence.
